Strings.explanation: A String in Java is an object that represents a sequence of characters. Strings are immutable, meaning their contents cannot be changed after creation. Java provides many built-in String methods for searching, comparing, extracting, replacing, splitting, converting, formatting, and manipulating text.

String Introduction.explanation: String is a class in java.lang used to represent text. String literals can be created using double quotes, while strings can also be created using the String class constructor.
String Introduction.example: String name = "Java" stores the text Java.
points_to_remember: String belongs to the java.lang package.
String objects are immutable.
String literals use double quotes.
String can also be created using new String().

String Immutability.explanation: Strings are immutable in Java. Once a String object is created, its contents cannot be changed. Operations that appear to modify a String actually create a new String.
String Immutability.example: The first concat() does not change text because its returned String is not assigned.
points_to_remember: String objects cannot be modified after creation.
String methods generally return a new String.
Assign the returned value if you want to keep the modified String.
String immutability makes strings suitable for safe sharing.

String Length.explanation: The length() method returns the number of UTF-16 code units contained in a String.
points_to_remember: length() returns an integer.
Spaces are included in the length.
String length is accessed using length().
Arrays use length while Strings use length().

charAt().explanation: charAt() returns the character located at a specified zero-based index.
charAt().example: The result is 'v' because v is at index 2.
points_to_remember: Indexing starts from 0.
charAt() returns a char.
An invalid index causes StringIndexOutOfBoundsException.

codePointAt().explanation: codePointAt() returns the Unicode code point at a specified index.
codePointAt().example: The Unicode code point of 'J' is 74.
points_to_remember: Returns an int Unicode code point.
Useful when working with Unicode characters.
It differs from charAt(), which returns a UTF-16 char.

substring().explanation: substring() extracts a portion of a String and returns a new String.
substring().example: substring(0, 5) returns Hello and substring(6) returns Java.
points_to_remember: The starting index is inclusive.
The ending index is exclusive.
substring(start) extracts from start to the end.
The original String remains unchanged.

equals().explanation: equals() compares two String objects based on their actual character contents.
equals().example: The result is true because both strings contain the same characters.
points_to_remember: equals() compares contents.
It is case-sensitive.
Use equals() instead of == when comparing String contents.

equalsIgnoreCase().explanation: equalsIgnoreCase() compares two strings without considering differences in letter case.
equalsIgnoreCase().example: The result is true because case differences are ignored.
points_to_remember: Case differences are ignored.
Character content is still compared.
It is useful for case-insensitive comparisons.

compareTo().explanation: compareTo() compares two strings lexicographically and returns a negative, zero, or positive integer.
compareTo().example: Apple comes before Banana lexicographically, so the result is negative.
points_to_remember: Returns 0 when strings are equal.
Returns a negative value when the first string comes before the second.
Returns a positive value when the first string comes after the second.
Comparison is case-sensitive.

compareToIgnoreCase().explanation: compareToIgnoreCase() performs lexicographical comparison without considering letter-case differences.
compareToIgnoreCase().example: The result is 0 because the strings are equivalent when case is ignored.
points_to_remember: Case differences are ignored.
Returns 0 for equivalent strings.
Useful for case-insensitive sorting or comparison.

contains().explanation: contains() checks whether a String contains a specified sequence of characters.
contains().example: The result is true because Program occurs inside the string.
points_to_remember: contains() returns boolean.
It is case-sensitive.
It accepts a CharSequence.

startsWith().explanation: startsWith() checks whether a String begins with a specified prefix.
startsWith().example: The result is true because the String begins with Java.
points_to_remember: startsWith() returns boolean.
It is case-sensitive.
A starting offset can also be supplied.

endsWith().explanation: endsWith() checks whether a String ends with a specified suffix.
endsWith().example: The result is true because the file name ends with .pdf.
points_to_remember: endsWith() returns boolean.
It is case-sensitive.
Useful for checking file extensions and suffixes.

indexOf().explanation: indexOf() returns the index of the first occurrence of a specified character or substring.
indexOf().example: indexOf() can find the first position of a character or substring.
points_to_remember: Returns the first matching index.
Returns -1 when no match is found.
Overloads exist for char and String.
A starting index can also be supplied.

lastIndexOf().explanation: lastIndexOf() returns the index of the last occurrence of a specified character or substring.
lastIndexOf().example: The method returns the position of the final occurrence of the specified character.
points_to_remember: Searches from the end of the String.
Returns -1 when no match is found.
Can search for characters or substrings.

replace().explanation: replace() replaces occurrences of a character or literal character sequence with another value.
replace().example: The result is Java is powerful.
points_to_remember: replace() performs literal replacement.
It does not modify the original String.
It returns a new String.

replaceFirst().explanation: replaceFirst() replaces the first substring that matches a regular expression.
replaceFirst().example: Only the first occurrence is replaced.
points_to_remember: The first matching substring is replaced.
The first argument is interpreted as a regular expression.
Use replace() when regular-expression behavior is not required.

replaceAll().explanation: replaceAll() replaces every substring that matches a regular expression.
replaceAll().example: All numeric sequences are removed from the String.
points_to_remember: replaceAll() uses regular expressions.
All matching portions are replaced.
It returns a new String.
Use replace() for simple literal replacement.

toUpperCase().explanation: toUpperCase() converts characters in a String to uppercase using the default locale unless a locale is explicitly supplied.
points_to_remember: Returns a new String.
The original String is unchanged.
Locale-sensitive behavior can matter for certain languages.

toLowerCase().explanation: toLowerCase() converts characters in a String to lowercase using the default locale unless a locale is explicitly supplied.
points_to_remember: Returns a new String.
The original String is unchanged.
Locale-sensitive behavior can matter for certain languages.

trim().explanation: trim() removes leading and trailing characters less than or equal to the ASCII space character.
trim().example: The result is Java without the leading and trailing spaces.
points_to_remember: trim() removes leading and trailing basic space characters.
It does not remove whitespace from the middle.
The original String is unchanged.

strip().explanation: strip() removes leading and trailing Unicode whitespace and is generally more Unicode-aware than trim().
strip().example: The leading and trailing whitespace is removed.
points_to_remember: strip() is available in modern Java versions.
It handles Unicode whitespace.
stripLeading() removes only leading whitespace.
stripTrailing() removes only trailing whitespace.

isEmpty().explanation: isEmpty() checks whether a String has zero characters.
isEmpty().example: The result is true because the String contains no characters.
points_to_remember: isEmpty() returns true only when length() is zero.
A String containing spaces is not empty.

isBlank().explanation: isBlank() checks whether a String is empty or contains only Unicode whitespace characters.
isBlank().example: The result is true because the String contains only whitespace.
points_to_remember: isBlank() is available in modern Java versions.
An empty String is blank.
A whitespace-only String is blank.
isEmpty() and isBlank() are not equivalent.

concat().explanation: concat() joins another String to the end of the current String.
points_to_remember: concat() returns a new String.
The original String remains unchanged.
The + operator can also be used for String concatenation.

String.join().explanation: String.join() combines multiple strings using a specified delimiter.
String.join().example: The result is Java, Python, C++.
points_to_remember: join() inserts the delimiter between elements.
It is useful for creating comma-separated or delimiter-separated text.
It can work with multiple CharSequence values or an Iterable.

split().explanation: split() divides a String into an array of substrings using a regular expression as the delimiter.
split().example: The String is divided into Java, Python, and C++.
points_to_remember: split() returns a String array.
The delimiter is treated as a regular expression.
A limit can be supplied.
Special regex characters may need escaping.

matches().explanation: matches() checks whether the entire String matches a specified regular expression.
matches().example: The result is true because the complete String contains only digits.
points_to_remember: matches() uses regular expressions.
The entire String must match the pattern.
It returns a boolean.

toCharArray().explanation: toCharArray() converts a String into a new character array.
toCharArray().example: The String Java becomes the character array ['J', 'a', 'v', 'a'].
points_to_remember: Returns a new char array.
Changes to the array do not modify the original String.
Useful when character-level array processing is required.

getBytes().explanation: getBytes() converts a String into a byte array using a character encoding.
getBytes().example: The String can be encoded as UTF-8 bytes for file, network, or other byte-based operations.
points_to_remember: Encoding determines how characters are converted to bytes.
UTF-8 is commonly used.
Using an explicit charset avoids platform-dependent encoding behavior.

String.valueOf().explanation: String.valueOf() converts primitive values and objects into their String representation.
points_to_remember: Supports primitive values and objects.
Useful for explicit conversion to String.
String concatenation can also perform automatic conversion.

String.format().explanation: String.format() creates a formatted String using format specifiers.
String.format().example: The result is Name: Alice, Age: 20.
points_to_remember: %s is commonly used for strings.
%d is commonly used for integers.
%f is commonly used for floating-point values.
Formatting creates a new String.

formatted().explanation: formatted() formats a String using the String itself as the format string.
formatted().example: The result is Name: Alice, Age: 20.
points_to_remember: formatted() provides an instance-style formatting API.
It uses the same general format specifier rules as String.format().
It is available in modern Java versions.

repeat().explanation: repeat() returns a String containing the original sequence repeated a specified number of times.
repeat().example: The result is Java Java Java.
points_to_remember: The repeat count must not be negative.
Repeating zero times produces an empty String.
repeat() is available in modern Java versions.

indent().explanation: indent() adjusts the indentation of each line in a String.
indent().example: Each line receives the specified indentation.
points_to_remember: Positive values add indentation.
Negative values can remove indentation.
It works line by line.

lines().explanation: lines() returns a Stream of lines from a String.
lines().example: Each line can be processed individually using the returned Stream.
points_to_remember: lines() returns a Stream<String>.
It is useful for processing multiline text.
It is available in modern Java versions.

transform().explanation: transform() applies a function to a String and returns the function's result.
transform().example: The String java is transformed into JAVA.
points_to_remember: transform() accepts a Function.
It can be used to build readable transformation pipelines.
The returned value can be a type other than String.

intern().explanation: intern() returns the canonical representation of a String from the String pool.
intern().example: The result is true because b refers to the pooled representation of Java.
points_to_remember: String literals are stored in the String pool.
intern() returns a pooled representation.
Use intern() deliberately because excessive interning can affect memory usage.

String Pool.explanation: The String pool is a JVM-managed area that allows identical String literals to share the same String object.
String Pool.example: Both variables normally refer to the same pooled String literal.
points_to_remember: String literals are pooled.
String pooling can reduce duplicate String objects.
== compares references, not String contents.
Use equals() to compare String contents.

StringBuilder.explanation: StringBuilder is a mutable sequence of characters designed for efficient String construction and modification, especially when many changes are required.
StringBuilder.example: StringBuilder can efficiently construct a String through multiple modifications.
points_to_remember: StringBuilder is mutable.
append() adds content.
insert() inserts content at an index.
StringBuilder is generally preferred for repeated String modifications in a single thread.

StringBuilder Built-in Methods.explanation: StringBuilder provides many mutable text operations such as append, insert, delete, replace, reverse, and setCharAt.
StringBuilder Built-in Methods.example: StringBuilder allows multiple modifications without creating a new String for every operation.
points_to_remember: append() adds content.
insert() adds content at an index.
delete() removes a range.
replace() replaces a range.
reverse() reverses the sequence.
setCharAt() changes a character.
capacity() returns the current capacity.

StringBuffer.explanation: StringBuffer is a mutable character sequence similar to StringBuilder, with synchronized methods intended for use where thread-safe mutable string operations are required.
StringBuffer.example: StringBuffer can be used when synchronized mutable text operations are required.
points_to_remember: StringBuffer is mutable.
Its methods are synchronized.
StringBuilder is generally preferred when synchronization is unnecessary.
It provides methods similar to StringBuilder.

summary: String is an immutable sequence of characters.
length() returns the number of UTF-16 code units in the String.
equals() should be used to compare String contents.
== compares String references rather than String contents.
substring() extracts a portion of a String.
indexOf() and lastIndexOf() search for characters or substrings.
replace(), replaceFirst(), and replaceAll() replace String content.
split() divides a String into an array.
contains(), startsWith(), and endsWith() perform common searches.
trim() and strip() remove leading and trailing whitespace with different definitions.
String.join() combines multiple strings using a delimiter.
String.format() and formatted() create formatted strings.
StringBuilder provides efficient mutable String manipulation.
StringBuffer provides synchronized mutable String manipulation.
String provides extensive Unicode and code-point APIs.
